Lesson 9.1

Messages, Streams, and Multiplayer

Client and server

Section titled “Client and server”

A client is the game program running on a player’s device. It reads the player’s keyboard or controller, draws the world, and exchanges messages with another program over the network.

A server is a program that receives requests from clients and provides a service to them. A game server might keep track of who has joined a match, calculate player movement and damage, and send the resulting positions and health to the connected players. The computer running that program is also often called “the server.” The program can run on a rented machine, on one player’s computer, or beside your client on the same computer during a local test.

Imagine a match where the server calculates movement. It stores a player at (10, 15). The player’s client sends “move north.” The server checks whether the destination is inside the map and free of a wall. If the move is possible, it changes its stored position to (10, 14) and sends that position to the clients. Each client updates the character it draws. If a wall blocks the move, the server keeps (10, 15) and reports that position instead.

In this example Client program Server program
Input Notices the north key press and sends a move request. Receives the request and identifies the player who sent it.
Simulation May predict movement to make the controls feel responsive. Checks the destination and updates the match’s stored position.
Display Draws the player at the latest known or predicted position. Sends position updates; a dedicated server usually draws no game window.

Clarification: Client and server name the programs’ jobs. They do not require two computers: a local test can run both programs on one machine and connect them through loopback.

This is one common arrangement, called a server-authoritative simulation: the server’s accepted position is the one the clients eventually use. Other games give the server a smaller job, such as hosting a lobby or forwarding players’ inputs. A server does not necessarily simulate every part of a game, and the clients do not necessarily hold identical or complete copies of its data.

This chapter follows that message from intent to bytes, from captured bytes to a parsed event, and from one event to a legal session transition. A local chat client and proxy put the pieces together. The final lessons ask how two programs on one computer can exchange equally well-defined messages without using a network socket.

The client’s “move north” is an intent: a request for a change, not the final truth. The reply reports what the server actually accepted. If a wall blocked the move, the reply might still say (10, 15), and the client would correct its display.

These programs have separate memory. Changing a position in the client’s memory does not directly change the server’s stored position. They communicate by sending bytes. A client may display a predicted move while it waits, then correct that display when the server’s reply arrives. The next question is how the reply’s bytes become one complete message at the other end.

Peer-to-peer describes who communicates with whom

Section titled “Peer-to-peer describes who communicates with whom”

In a peer-to-peer arrangement, players’ programs can exchange messages directly. A lobby service may still introduce them, and a relay may carry bytes when a direct connection is unavailable. Neither service must calculate the match.

A player who hosts a server on their own computer still runs a client/server arrangement if that server accepts movement and sends the final positions. The location of the program does not change its job.

Example arrangement Message path Who calculates the accepted position here?
Dedicated game server Each client talks to the server program. The server program.
Player hosts the game server Clients talk to the server on a player’s computer. That server program.
Peers exchange inputs Players exchange the same ordered input history. Each peer runs the agreed deterministic simulation.

The last row describes one particular design, often called lockstep. Peer-to-peer does not automatically mean lockstep: another design can give one peer responsibility for an object or use different ways to resolve conflicts. Always ask two separate questions: where do messages go, and whose result is accepted? Direct communication alone does not prove which copy owns a gold value.

The same movement request, three arrangements. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

start at (10, 15)
request move north
deliver input to the selected participants
check destination against the shared map
accept (10, 14) or keep (10, 15)
draw the accepted position

Each player draws (10, 14). The server’s accepted result determines the final position, even when that program runs on a player’s computer.

Final values: arrangement = dedicated; destination = clear; position = (10, 14); calculator = dedicated server program; blocked = false.

Clarification: A server is a program with a job. A peer is another participant. Hosting on a player’s computer and exchanging directly between peers describe different choices.

Topology cheatsheet: client/server identifies service roles; peer-to-peer describes communication between participants; authority identifies the accepted result. A topology label alone cannot answer all three questions.

TCP is a stream

Section titled “TCP is a stream”

TCP is a common transport for a connection between the two programs. It delivers an ordered stream of bytes. A program calls read to take some bytes that have arrived from that stream. TCP does not preserve the game’s message boundaries for that call.

One call to read may return:

  • half of one message;
  • exactly one message;
  • one message plus part of the next;
  • several messages.

Concretely: if the sender writes two length-prefixed messages back to back, the receiver has no say in how they turn up.

Neither read lands on a message boundary. The receiver has to hold what it has in a buffer, remove complete messages when enough bytes have arrived, and keep the leftover for next time. A parser that assumes one read equals one message works flawlessly over a fast loopback connection while you are testing, then breaks the moment timing changes.

This is why a protocol needs framing.

stream supplies incoming bytes and max_size is the caller’s permitted payload limit. A successful call returns one payload as a Vec<u8>; a truncated header or payload produces an I/O error through ?. For a header 00 00 00 02 followed by 41 42, the returned vector contains just 41 42. The maximum size prevents a bad length field from requesting absurd amounts of memory. This blocking helper also needs an appropriate timeout on a real socket so a peer cannot make it wait indefinitely.

TCP reliability ends at delivering an ordered byte stream to the receiving socket. It does not prove the application parsed a complete message, accepted the request, saved the state, or sent a meaningful reply. The application must provide those guarantees. An acknowledgment can report acceptance, a request ID can identify a repeated request, and a timeout can tell the client when to stop waiting. Decide whether a retry repeats the same request or starts a new one before implementing it.

Byte order is part of the protocol

Section titled “Byte order is part of the protocol”

The same integer has more than one possible byte order. Decimal 258 is 1 × 256 + 2, so as a four-byte number it has one byte worth 256 (01), one byte worth 1 (02), and two zero bytes. Wesnoth’s four-byte frame length is big endian, which puts the byte worth the most first:

On little-endian x86 memory, a native u32 with the same value would usually appear in the opposite order:

Read with the wrong order, the wire bytes 00 00 01 02 become 0x02010000, which is 2 × 16,777,216 + 1 × 65,536 = 33,619,968: a frame length of more than 33 million bytes. Network code must follow the protocol, not the host CPU’s default. That is why the reader uses u32::from_be_bytes rather than a pointer cast.

Packets and protocols

Section titled “Packets and protocols”

A packet is a chunk of bytes sent across a network. That part is straightforward.

A protocol specifies how programs communicate: how to separate messages, decode their fields, order the conversation, and respond to invalid input. Both programs need matching answers to these four questions:

  1. Where does one message end and the next begin? A TCP connection is one long stream of bytes with no natural gaps, so something has to mark the boundaries.
  2. What is each part of a message? Which bytes are the length, which are the message type, which are the payload, and how each of those is encoded.
  3. Which messages are allowed right now? A login reply makes no sense before a login request. People routinely forget this is part of the protocol at all.
  4. What happens when something is wrong? An unknown message type, a length that does not fit, a message arriving out of turn.

None of that can be worked out by staring at the bytes, because none of it is written in them. Both programs have to know it in advance. That is precisely why reverse engineering a protocol means recovering those four answers — and why a byte layout on its own only ever answers the second one.

Note

📦 Watch for: the same bytes can be perfectly valid at one point in a conversation and meaningless at another. A protocol model has to check when a message is legal, not only what it contains.

A simple framed message might contain:

A typed message models the decoded meaning:

This enum is a declaration fragment, not a network reader. After framing and validation, a parser can turn a move’s fields into Message::Move with a unit ID and two coordinates; the game logic receives named values instead of raw byte offsets. The bytes are untrusted until parsing succeeds.

One message is wrapped in several layers

Section titled “One message is wrapped in several layers”

Several layers cooperate when the bot sends one chat message:

WML, Wesnoth Markup Language, is Wesnoth’s own tagged text format for structured data — chat messages, maps, units, and more all get written as bracketed tags such as [message] and [/message] wrapping quoted key="value" fields. It is the serialization format this chapter keeps reversing.

When something fails, ask which layer broke. A correct TCP connection does not prove the WML is valid. A valid gzip stream does not prove the length prefix used the right byte order.

The receiver undoes the layers in the opposite order, and each step has its own way to fail:

Serialization turns structured values into bytes. Framing tells the receiver where one serialized message ends. Transport moves bytes between endpoints. Keeping those jobs separate makes both the explanation and the code easier to test.

Messages can feed a data pipeline

Section titled “Messages can feed a data pipeline”

A multiplayer service handles more than packets. It may keep durable account and inventory records in a database, reuse expensive results in a cache, and build a search index for queries such as finding a match by region and mode. Those are different access patterns: keep data across restarts, avoid repeating work, and find selected records efficiently. They are not three names for the authoritative state of a running match.

Processing is asynchronous when the sender can continue before the work finishes. A request can enter a queue, then a worker handles it later. A queue acknowledgment might mean “received”; it does not by itself mean “validated, applied, and saved.” The protocol must say which stage each reply confirms.

There are also two common ways to process a sequence of events:

Processing style Game-service example What it must account for
Stream processing Update a match’s statistics as accepted events arrive Ordering, late events, duplicates, and how quickly the result is needed
Batch processing Recompute a leaderboard from a collected set of finished-match results Which results belong to the batch, when it runs, and how to repeat it safely

“Stream processing” here means processing ongoing events; it does not mean the TCP byte stream discussed earlier. A service can obtain events from many connections, files, or queues. A batch deliberately waits for a group of data and processes that group together. Neither approach implies that a game can wait for a leaderboard job before processing a player’s movement or damage.

For example, a match event might carry match_id, event_id, and a score change. If a sender retries it after a lost acknowledgment, the receiver must recognise the same event rather than add the score twice. Event identity and retry behaviour belong to the model and protocol, not to whether TCP delivered the underlying bytes correctly.

Modularity and scaling follow the dependencies

Section titled “Modularity and scaling follow the dependencies”

Keep receiving bytes, parsing messages, checking requested actions, and saving results as identifiable jobs. Then measure where time is spent. A slow disk write, repeated full-player search, and long logging operation need different remedies; adding workers does not remove a shared bottleneck automatically.

Several independent matches can often run on separate workers. Within one match, operations on shared state still need a defined order. Moving one job to another process also adds a message boundary, possible failures, and delay. Start with a small correct local service, preserve these contracts, and distribute work when measurements and the use case justify it.

Bound queues as well as messages. If input arrives faster than it can be processed, an unbounded queue consumes memory and makes results increasingly stale. A newer position snapshot may replace an older one under a documented policy; a one-time item grant needs different handling. That is a decision about message meaning: discarding an old position can be useful, but discarding an unprocessed item grant loses the item.

Design the backend for one match

Section titled “Design the backend for one match”

A player logs in, joins match 42, and buys an item for 300 coins. The game backend is the set of services behind those actions. Separating their jobs explains why a working socket alone cannot prove a successful purchase.

From login to the live world

Section titled “From login to the live world”

Authentication establishes the player’s identity. A session lets later requests refer to that authenticated login; it can outlive one TCP connection. A matchmaker groups compatible players and arranges a match location. It does not calculate their movement. Microsoft’s PlayFab matchmaking overview illustrates that service role.

An API gateway routes requests to the appropriate service. Middleware performs shared checks along that route: validate the session, bound the request, enforce its permissions, and record its outcome. A load balancer can spread these entry requests across equivalent gateway instances. The authoritative match server owns match 42’s accepted positions and damage; route its commands to that owner instead of a randomly chosen empty worker. These are logical jobs, which a small project can combine in one program.

Put each value in the right store

Section titled “Put each value in the right store”

A database keeps structured, durable account balances and inventory. Object storage keeps larger files addressed by keys, such as versioned patches and replay recordings. A cache reuses a result that can be rebuilt; a CDN, or content delivery network, brings eligible asset copies closer to players. An asset cache hit can avoid an origin fetch, as Cloudflare’s request lifecycle explains. Personal account responses need separate authorization and cache rules. A cached lobby count is useful; its old balance must not authorize a new purchase.

One purchase, one effect

Section titled “One purchase, one effect”

The player has 1,000 coins. Request P7 asks for the 300-coin item. Validate the server’s price and current balance, debit to 700, grant the item, and record P7’s result inside one transaction: either that whole change commits or none does. Concurrent requests also need appropriate isolation or locking; merely surrounding unsafe read-then-write logic with a transaction is insufficient. PostgreSQL’s isolation guide explains these concurrency guarantees and possible transaction retries.

If the reply is lost, retry the same request ID. Idempotency means that repeat has the same effect: return the recorded result, without another debit or item. Scope the ID to its account, reject a changed payload under the same ID, and save the receipt atomically with the effect.

Consistency describes which writes a read can observe. A strongly consistent read respects completed writes within its promised scope. A weaker read can return an older replica or cache value. Eventual consistency promises convergence when updates stop and propagation succeeds, not a fixed maximum delay. Currency authorization needs a current protected decision; a leaderboard can tolerate a clearly dated older view. Cosmos DB’s consistency definitions show why these guarantees must be stated explicitly.

Optional: explore the smaller concurrency problem below. Starting at 1,000, a reward of 500 and purchase of 300 should leave 1,200. Overlapping reads and writes can lose one change. Its local lock illustrates ordering; a backend must enforce its database transaction rules across all participating processes.

This simulation needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it works through the same numbers.

More matches, with explicit ownership

Section titled “More matches, with explicit ownership”

Sharding partitions work or records by a key: independent matches can run on different workers. A shared world crossing shard boundaries additionally needs ownership handoffs and ordered cross-boundary actions. Azure’s sharding pattern describes the partitioning tradeoff.

Coordination records which worker owns match 42. On failure, a replacement needs recoverable state and a new ownership generation; an expired worker must be prevented from committing late writes. Electing a replacement alone cannot reconstruct lost match state. Leader-election guidance explains leases and their failure limits. Retried result events also need persistent event IDs to avoid awarding the same win twice.

Spend the latency budget where it matters

Section titled “Spend the latency budget where it matters”

A toy 60-tick-per-second server has about 16.7 milliseconds per simulation step. That budget is distinct from network round-trip delay. Keep slow replay uploads and leaderboard work outside the movement path. Measure queue depth, bytes per player, and slow-tail latency before optimizing. Spatial indexes can reduce repeated full-world searches; smaller state deltas reduce bandwidth, while compression spends CPU time. Extra workers cannot repair an undefined ownership rule or an overloaded shared database.

UDP is made of datagrams

Section titled “UDP is made of datagrams”

UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not guarantee delivery, order, or uniqueness. Fast games often tolerate those tradeoffs for time-sensitive state.

A later position update can make an older one useless, so freshness may matter more than retransmission. In contrast, a one-time inventory change may need explicit ordering and acknowledgment. Choose behavior per message kind instead of labeling an entire game “reliable” or “unreliable.”

Do not assume a game uses only one protocol. It might use TCP for login/chat and UDP for movement.

Ports and sockets

Section titled “Ports and sockets”

A socket represents a network endpoint. This complete helper opens a TCP connection to our local test server, or returns an error:

127.0.0.1 means the same computer; 15000 selects the server’s listening port. We use loopback and a local test server for this section. A successful result is a connected stream; framing and protocol checks still remain.

Encryption changes what you can see

Section titled “Encryption changes what you can see”

If a protocol uses modern encryption correctly, a packet capture shows encrypted bytes, addresses, sizes, and timing—not readable messages. Do not try to defeat encryption or certificate checks.

For learning, use:

  • your own toy protocol;
  • a local open-source server;
  • captured bytes provided by a challenge;
  • application logs you control.

Captures in this chapter stay local

Section titled “Captures in this chapter stay local”

The capture, replay, and proxy examples use loopback or a local test server. That keeps timing, state changes, and failures observable while you learn what each protocol layer contributes.

Now that the message boundary and its byte order have a purpose, Lesson 9.3 records a real local exchange and asks which captured bytes correspond to one controlled action.

Lesson 9.2

What the Server Can See

The server receives requests and runs the shared simulation. It can see the accepted position, inventory, cooldowns, and command history. It does not directly see what a player was thinking or every program on their computer. Build checks around what the server actually knows.

Validate an action in the current world

Section titled “Validate an action in the current world”

Validation checks types, ranges, and current game state before data can change the world. For a movement command, check the input’s finite numeric values and allowed range. Then simulate movement using server-owned speed, collision, and time. A client-reported final position cannot replace those steps.

The permitted range must match the movement being simulated. A knockback, vehicle, or teleport ability changes what movement is possible. Checking only a single speed ceiling can mistake a valid ability for cheating.

A purchase needs the player’s identity, the item’s current price, and their server-owned balance. Apply the debit and reward together. Otherwise, two concurrent requests could both spend the same old balance, like the lost-update problem in the threading lessons.

Bound how much work a client causes

Section titled “Bound how much work a client causes”

A rate limit bounds work or requests within a period. Limit expensive queries, parser allocation, and accepted actions separately. Receiving a burst after network delay does not mean the player earned extra simulation time.

Lesson 9.1 separated framing, parsing, and permitted messages in each session state. Keep that order here. Reject an invalid length before allocating its claimed buffer. Reject an action in the wrong session state before changing the world. Handle duplicates according to the action’s documented retry behavior.

Record the original server timing as well as the command’s claimed timing. Source’s lag-compensation checks in Lesson 9.10 illustrate why the server must bound and compare those claims rather than accepting arbitrary history.

Withhold information the client does not need

Section titled “Withhold information the client does not need”

Fog of war limits what a client learns: hide game information until the player is entitled to observe it. A server that sends every hidden enemy position and merely hides the corresponding drawing has already disclosed the data.

In the toy picture, a wall blocks the observer’s sightline. The server knows the enemy’s position but sends none to this client. The enemy moves above the wall. Only after the new sightline clears the wall does its position enter the client’s observation.

Filter state before sending the message. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

read the selected inputs
evaluate each stated condition
combine the required conditions
perform the effect only when accepted
otherwise retain the old state
report the result and its limits

Result: the outgoing record has no hidden-enemy position. Client drawing cannot recover an absent field.

Final values: position = 8; wall = yes; line_clear = false; accepted = false; sent_position = absent.

Real visibility systems must account for more than this one line. Animation, sound, team information, latency, and other players’ perspectives can make an entity relevant. Reveal it early enough to avoid visible pop-in, but do not disclose unrelated hidden state. Lesson 7.8 applies the same server-owned visibility decision to radar markers.

Alternative: Ask what the client needs to draw now. Construct that observation on the server before sending it.

Replays preserve useful context

Section titled “Replays preserve useful context”

A replay records enough accepted state and input to inspect a past sequence. Store the game version and the timing used to apply commands alongside it. A video from one client can omit information available to the server and include prediction or interpolation differences.

Replay review helps distinguish an impossible state from an unusual but legal tactic. It also reveals what a check was unable to observe. A replay that omits raw input edges cannot prove the timing of those omitted edges.

Machine learning fits a model to examples instead of using only hand- written checks. It can rank large numbers of replay segments for review. Its training labels can contain mistakes, and a new game update can change the input distribution. Test on held-out legitimate matches, different devices, and the updated game. A model score is a signal with measured limits, not an explanation of guilt by itself.

Lesson 9.3

Protocol Capture and Message Framing

Separate network layers before capturing

Section titled “Separate network layers before capturing”

Lesson 9.1 showed that one game message can arrive across two TCP reads. A packet capture lets us inspect the bytes on the way, but its packet rows are not automatically game-message rows. We will send one distinctive lobby message, then follow its bytes in both directions.

An application message is not the same thing as an IP packet or TCP segment. Each layer has a different job:

TCP may split one game message across several segments or combine bytes from several messages in one segment. Retransmissions can repeat packet data. The receiving application sees an ordered stream, so protocol parsing needs its own framing rule such as a length prefix or delimiter.

This board needs JavaScript to move things around. Here is the lesson’s sorting:

Game protocol message
  • A login message. Login, chat and lobby updates are game protocol messages. That is the level your parser works at.
  • A length prefix saying where a message ends. The receiver sees an ordered stream, so protocol parsing needs its own framing rule such as a length prefix or a delimiter.
TCP byte stream
  • Bytes arrive in order, none missing. That is the TCP promise: an ordered, reliable stream of bytes between two sockets.
  • The four-tuple: source address and port, destination address and port. A TCP connection is identified by these four values, which is why one connection reads differently in each direction.
  • One game message split across several segments. TCP may split one message across several segments or combine bytes from several messages into one. A segment boundary is not a message boundary.
IP packet
  • Routing data between host addresses. Moving data between hosts by address is the IP packet’s job.
Capture
  • The row you see in the capture tool. A capture records bytes and timing at one point. A row there is not automatically a game message, and it cannot say why it was sent.

A socket is an operating-system object representing one endpoint. A TCP connection is identified by source address, source port, destination address, and destination port—the four-tuple used below.

Follow a join request beyond loopback

Section titled “Follow a join request beyond loopback”

Our capture stays local. To understand the wider journey, imagine a client joining match 42 and downloading its map from assets.example. Configuration, name lookup, delivery, and game permission solve different parts of that trip.

Find a destination before connecting

Section titled “Find a destination before connecting”

On a typical IPv4 LAN, DHCP gives a device an address lease and network configuration; options can supply a router and DNS servers. It configures the device, not the remote game’s identity. DHCP and its options specify that exchange. Static configuration and other address-assignment systems are also possible.

DNS resolves a name such as assets.example to records including IP addresses. A resolver can reuse an answer until its cache lifetime expires; name resolution does not deliver the map. The client then connects to the chosen endpoint. DNS concepts explain this separate lookup.

HTTP is the web’s request/response protocol. HTTPS carries that exchange over an authenticated, encrypted connection. A CDN can serve a cached map from an edge location. A cache miss may require an origin fetch; DNS answer caching and content caching have different lifetimes. Account requests still need their own authentication and cache policy. Cloudflare’s request journey shows these boundaries.

Wrap the bytes across a LAN

Section titled “Wrap the bytes across a LAN”

A LAN, or local area network, joins nearby devices through links such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi. In this example, an Ethernet frame carries an IP packet, which carries a UDP datagram, which carries game bytes. This wrapping is encapsulation. A switch forwards link frames; a router forwards the IP packet onto another link with a new link frame. Physical signaling carries the bits on each link.

The OSI model names seven conceptual layers: application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link, and physical. The Internet’s TCP/IP model commonly groups application work, transport, Internet/IP, and link work. These models describe responsibilities, not seven mandatory headers. Our existing layer board remains useful: identify the job before assigning a name. Internet host requirements organize the protocol suite by these responsibilities.

Choose the delivery contract, then the application protocol

Section titled “Choose the delivery contract, then the application protocol”

If middle bytes are lost, TCP recovers them before exposing later bytes in its ordered stream. UDP can deliver a later datagram without the missing one; the game decides whether to replace stale state or add its own recovery. Neither transport acknowledgment proves the server accepted a purchase. TCP and UDP specify those different contracts.

A socket is the local operating-system endpoint already introduced above. A WebSocket is a two-way framed-message protocol, useful for browser lobby chat. The RFC 6455 handshake uses HTTP/1.1 Upgrade; wss protects the exchange with TLS, Transport Layer Security, which authenticates the server and protects data in transit. HTTP/3 also has a WebSocket mapping, so an Upgrade handshake is not universal. Game authorization remains separate.

QUIC v1 runs over UDP but supplies its own reliable streams and loss recovery, using TLS 1.3 for connection security. HTTP/3 maps HTTP requests and responses onto QUIC. Loss affecting one stream need not block unrelated stream delivery, although streams share connection congestion limits. QUIC is not “unreliable HTTP,” and HTTP/3 is not a synonym for every game’s UDP protocol. The standards are QUIC v1, QUIC with TLS, and HTTP/3.

Clarification: A socket names an endpoint; WebSocket names a message protocol. QUIC builds reliable streams over UDP. An encrypted channel still needs game-specific identity and action checks.

Other names belong at other boundaries

Section titled “Other names belong at other boundaries”

Publishing the map might use FTP, which separates control and data connections, or SFTP, which transfers files over encrypted SSH. SFTP is different from FTPS, FTP secured with TLS. A web server might use FastCGI to pass requests to a persistent application worker; the player’s side still uses HTTP. Web3 applications may use blockchain-backed records, but a ledger is not a replacement for sockets or real-time match transport. Likewise, Base64 only encodes bytes: an encoded login value has not thereby been encrypted.

With those boundaries separate, return to the controlled local capture. We can now ask which interface, direction, and protocol layer produced each row.

Capture answers “what crossed,” not “why”

Section titled “Capture answers “what crossed,” not “why””

A network trace records bytes and timing at one capture point. It does not contain the sender’s variable names, the receiver’s interpretation, or any record of which UI action caused which packet. That link comes from changing one thing at a time:

  1. capture a quiet baseline;
  2. perform exactly one distinctive local action;
  3. repeat the action with one changed input;
  4. compare both directions and several repetitions;
  5. confirm the candidate fields in the open-source client or server.

TL;DR: A capture records traffic. Controlled actions and repeat comparisons connect those bytes to meaning.

Build a controlled capture

Section titled “Build a controlled capture”

Use the course’s local Wesnoth server setup or your own toy client and server. Keep both endpoints inside the lab VM.

Start Wireshark, choose the loopback adapter (Tip: On Windows the loopback adapter comes from Npcap, which the Wireshark installer offers. Wireshark lists it as “Adapter for loopback traffic capture”; older versions called it “Npcap Loopback Adapter”.) when client and server share the machine, and begin capture before connecting.

Capturing on the wrong interface produces an empty-looking experiment. Traffic to 127.0.0.1 stays on the loopback path rather than crossing the physical Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter.

Reduce noise

Section titled “Reduce noise”

Filter by the known local port. Wireshark has two filter boxes, and each has its own syntax for the same job:

Display filter (hides rows afterwards)

Capture filter (never records the rest)

A display filter can be changed at any time, because everything was recorded. A capture filter keeps the file small, but a packet it dropped cannot be recovered, so use the display filter while you are still learning what to look for.

For the Wesnoth 1.14.9 lab, keep 15000: that is wesnothd’s default listening port. Launch wesnothd.exe, choose Connect to Server in the game, and enter localhost:15000.

Perform the actions at known times, so each burst of packets can be matched to the action just before it:

A distinctive message such as hello-17 is easier to find than “hi.”

Direction matters

Section titled “Direction matters”

One connection has one four-tuple, and each direction reads it the other way round:

The client port is often temporary. The server port is the stable listening port.

The server first owns a listening socket on port 15000. Accepting a client creates a separate connected socket while the listener remains available for other clients. The client normally receives an ephemeral local port selected by Windows.

Follow the stream

Section titled “Follow the stream”

Wireshark’s “Follow TCP Stream” view reassembles TCP bytes for easier inspection (Tip: To open it, right-click any packet of the connection and choose Follow, then TCP Stream. The shortcut is Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T.).

Alternative: Picture TCP as one long ribbon: reads cut pieces from it, while your parser identifies complete messages.

Remember: this is still a stream, not necessarily a list of messages. Look for:

  • fixed-size headers;
  • length fields;
  • magic bytes;
  • repeated separators;
  • readable text;
  • compressed-looking regions;
  • request/response pairs.

“Follow TCP Stream” performs reassembly for inspection. Your client still has to handle partial reads: read() may return fewer bytes than requested even when more bytes will arrive later. read_exact is appropriate only after a validated frame length tells you exactly how many bytes belong to the next piece.

Reassembly also chooses an order from sequence numbers and removes retransmitted overlap. Preserve the original packet capture alongside any exported stream fixture so later questions about direction, timing, or retransmission can still be answered.

Export a tiny fixture

Section titled “Export a tiny fixture”

Save only the bytes for one clearly labeled action. A small binary fixture is excellent for parser tests.

Do not store secrets, account tokens, or other people’s traffic in fixtures.

Compare two captures

Section titled “Compare two captures”

Repeat the same action with exactly one changed input:

Compare lengths and differing byte ranges. If only one region changes, it may contain the text. If the whole payload changes, compression or encryption may be involved.

Narration: Changing only one input gives differences a clearer meaning than comparing two sessions where everything changed.

Identify the real Wesnoth handshake

Section titled “Identify the real Wesnoth handshake”

Add this display filter so Wireshark shows client/server data rather than every TCP acknowledgement:

The first client payload in a Wesnoth 1.14.9 connection is exactly four zero bytes:

Replay only those four bytes from a tiny TCP client. The local server responds with 41 bytes across the observed replies, proving that the zeros begin protocol negotiation. The next client frame identifies version 1.14.9; the following frame logs in with the chosen username.

After the four-byte frame length, both of those later frames begin with gzip magic bytes 1F 8B. For example, a captured version frame begins:

Do the same controlled capture with usernames IEUser and FFFAAAKKKEEE. The second name makes repeated-character compression easier to notice. Put together, the Wesnoth 1.14.9 connection works like this:

Capture facts the parser needs

Section titled “Capture facts the parser needs”

A useful frame fixture records:

  • the start of one frame;
  • the field that gives its size, or another reliable delimiter;
  • its direction;
  • one input and the bytes that changed because of it.

Lesson 9.4

Message Parsing and Serialization

Parse the real Wesnoth frame

Section titled “Parse the real Wesnoth frame”

The controlled captures from Wesnoth 1.14.9 reveal this frame:

The first four bytes do not include themselves in the length. If the header ends in 4E, the following gzip member is 78 bytes and the complete TCP payload is 82 bytes.

This four-byte prefix solves a problem TCP does not solve for us: message boundaries. A TCP read might return two header bytes now and the rest later, or it might return several complete frames together. The receiver therefore accumulates bytes until it has four, interprets the advertised length, then accumulates exactly that many payload bytes.

Big-endian means the most significant byte comes first. A length of 78 is hexadecimal 0x0000004E, so the wire contains 00 00 00 4E. u32::from_be_bytes documents that agreement directly; shifting bytes by hand would be harder to review.

The header is a claim from the sender, not permission to allocate whatever it asks for. Compare two headers followed by four bytes currently available:

The second header is four valid bytes, but its advertised size is not an acceptable frame for this parser. Code that allocates from that claim could request nearly four gigabytes. First reject any length above the configured maximum; only then wait for the advertised number of payload bytes, with a bounded buffer and a way to stop a stalled connection. Having only four payload bytes so far does not by itself prove a network frame is false, because TCP may deliver the rest later. After a complete frame is assembled, the parser checks its exact length before decoding it. This separates byte validation from the later question of whether the decoded chat message makes sense.

Keep five layers separate

Section titled “Keep five layers separate”

A protocol message has several nested layers. Each layer decodes the representation produced by the one outside it:

Each layer answers a different question. TCP delivers ordered bytes, not chat messages. Framing finds one complete compressed unit. Gzip recovers plain bytes. UTF-8 and WML give those bytes text structure. Only the game-level schema says that sender, room, and message form a chat event.

TL;DR: Framing, compression, text encoding, syntax, and session meaning can each fail independently.

This separation is a debugging tool. If the first four bytes advertise an impossible size, inspect framing. If decompression fails, inspect the wrapper and payload. If WML is malformed, inspect serialization. If valid WML is ignored by the game, inspect the expected message fields and connection state. Calling every failure a “packet problem” hides the layer that actually broke.

Read with a cursor

Section titled “Read with a cursor”

The four-byte length at the front of the captured frame must be read before the compressed body, and every read must stop at the captured buffer’s end. A cursor pairs the borrowed bytes with the next unread position. If a read fails, the position stays where it was, so an error cannot leave a parser halfway through a claimed field:

Alternative: The cursor is a bookmark: every accepted field advances it only after its bytes fit.

This cursor replaces direct indexing and hopeful conversion:

The original parser takes four header bytes, trusts their length, and indexes the payload. This is a failure example: a short header or a length beyond the captured buffer can panic; extra bytes are silently accepted.

The bounded cursor makes every read fallible and advances only after a valid range has been obtained. Requiring the cursor to finish at the end rejects trailing bytes in this one-frame format.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: treat malformed input as a parse error, and check the complete frame boundary.

Why this version?

Network input is allowed to be short, oversized, or malformed. Indexing panics when a boundary is wrong, and unwrap() erases the difference between bad input and a programmer bug. The cursor makes failure a normal Result, advances only after a successful bounded read, and lets the caller reject hidden trailing data after one complete frame.

The lifetime 'a says every slice returned by the cursor borrows from the original input. The cursor owns only a position number; it does not copy payloads or create references that outlive the frame.

take is the one place that advances parsing state. It first calculates the end with checked_add, asks the slice for a bounded range with get, and advances only after both checks succeed. This gives later field readers a simple promise: success consumes exactly the requested bytes; failure consumes nothing useful and returns an error.

try_into() converts a four-byte slice into [u8; 4], the fixed-size array required by from_be_bytes. The conversion can only succeed after take(4), but keeping the error path explicit makes the invariant visible instead of using unwrap().

Every read checks its boundary. Now decompress only the advertised bytes and cap the output:

There are two separate size limits here:

  • compressed_len limits how many bytes the parser accepts from the frame;
  • the take(MAX_FRAME + 1) wrapper limits how many bytes decompression may produce.

Both matter because a small compressed input can expand into a very large output. Reading one byte beyond the limit lets the parser distinguish “exactly at the limit” from “too large” without allocating an unbounded vector.

There is a third limit outside this pure function: the connection’s accumulated input buffer. A peer could advertise a legal one-megabyte frame and then send one byte every few seconds. The stream reader needs a maximum buffered size, read timeouts or cancellation, and a policy for a connection that never finishes its frame. Parsing bounds protect completed inputs; transport bounds protect the time and memory spent waiting for them.

The trailing-byte check makes this function parse one complete frame. Without it, a valid prefix could hide extra bytes that the caller mistakenly ignores. A streaming connection reader should split the stream into exact frame slices first and call this parser once per slice.

Decompressing a captured chat frame reveals readable Simple WML:

That is the actual structure we will rebuild.

Simple WML is a tree-shaped text format. Bracketed tags open and close nodes; quoted assignments store fields. This lesson handles the one chat-message shape needed by our local Wesnoth proxy. If you extend the tool to inspect maps, units, or arbitrary add-on messages, use a real tokenizer that handles escaping, nested nodes, repeated fields, and comments instead of adding more substring searches.

The receiver also has an expected schema, even when no formal schema file exists. That schema includes field names, allowed repetitions, value types, and which fields are required. The sender writes one version of that agreement; the receiver reads according to the version it understands.

When a game update adds a field, ask two different compatibility questions:

  • Can the new reader still understand old messages?
  • Can the old reader safely ignore or default the new field?

Those questions are not the same. A tolerant tree format may ignore an unknown optional field, but renaming a required field can break both directions. For a versioned research tool, keep captured fixtures from every supported game build and record which message shape each fixture uses instead of guessing that one parser is universal.

Compress and frame a real chat message

Section titled “Compress and frame a real chat message”

Use flate2:

With the gzip encoder available, the next function accepts a chat field as text and rejects quotes or line breaks that would change the simple WML structure. Only validated fields go into the message before compression and length framing:

Encoding runs the decoding pipeline in reverse:

  1. validate values before placing them inside quoted WML fields;
  2. serialize the typed message into UTF-8 text;
  3. finish the gzip stream so its footer is present;
  4. convert the compressed size to u32 without truncation;
  5. reserve one vector for header plus payload;
  6. append the big-endian length and compressed bytes.

Vec::with_capacity is an optimization, not a safety requirement. It avoids reallocating as the two pieces are appended. u32::try_from is a correctness requirement because as u32 could silently discard high bits for an oversized buffer.

GzEncoder produces the correct gzip wrapper; a plain zlib stream is not interchangeable here. The first two compressed bytes should be 1F 8B.

Gzip and zlib can both use the DEFLATE compression algorithm but wrap it in different headers and checksums. “Same compression algorithm” does not mean “same wire format.” Matching the observed wrapper is part of implementing the protocol.

Round-trip tests

Section titled “Round-trip tests”

Feed the serializer one sender and one message, then give its frame to the decoder. If the resulting WML still contains both values, the length, compression wrapper, UTF-8 text, and field quoting agree between these two functions for this case:

Also test an empty input, a truncated gzip member, an oversized length, invalid UTF-8 after decompression, extra trailing bytes, and rejected quote/newline characters.

Narration: Encoding then decoding your own message checks consistency; captured fixtures also check whether both directions share the same mistaken assumption.

A round trip proves that the encoder produces something this decoder accepts. It does not prove compatibility by itself, because two functions could share the same mistake. Keep at least one captured fixture from the real local session and verify that the decoder accepts it. Then send an encoded message to the controlled server and confirm that another capture has the expected four-byte prefix and gzip header.

Use a small failure matrix:

Test input Expected failure
Fewer than four bytes Truncated while reading the length
Length larger than remaining bytes Truncated while taking the payload
Length above the cap TooLarge before decompression
Valid frame plus one extra byte TrailingBytes
Broken gzip checksum InvalidGzip
Decompressed non-UTF-8 bytes InvalidUtf8
Quote inside a simple field Rejected before serialization

The goal is not merely to make one capture parse. It is to define exactly which byte strings are accepted and how malformed data fails.

The buildable protocol module is wesnoth_protocol.rs. It contains bounded frame reads, gzip encode/decode, output-size caps, strict trailing-byte checks, WML field sanitation, send_wml, encode_chat, and round-trip/error tests. Both the real chatbot and proxy import this same implementation instead of copying a shortened lesson version.

//! Bounds-checked Wesnoth 1.14.9 gzip/WML framing used by the local network labs.

use std::io::{self, Read, Write};

use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use flate2::{Compression, read::GzDecoder, write::GzEncoder};

pub const MAX_FRAME: usize = 1_048_576;

pub fn simple_field(value: &str) -> Result<&str> {
    anyhow::ensure!(
        !value
            .chars()
            .any(|character| matches!(character, '"' | '\n' | '\r')),
        "WML fields in this lab cannot contain quotes or newlines"
    );
    anyhow::ensure!(value.len() <= 512, "WML field is too long");
    Ok(value)
}

pub fn encode_frame(wml: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {
    anyhow::ensure!(wml.len() <= MAX_FRAME, "plain WML frame is too large");
    let mut encoder = GzEncoder::new(Vec::new(), Compression::default());
    encoder
        .write_all(wml.as_bytes())
        .context("could not gzip WML")?;
    let compressed = encoder.finish().context("could not finish gzip member")?;
    let length = u32::try_from(compressed.len()).context("compressed frame is too large")?;
    let mut frame = Vec::with_capacity(4 + compressed.len());
    frame.extend_from_slice(&length.to_be_bytes());
    frame.extend_from_slice(&compressed);
    Ok(frame)
}

pub fn decode_frame(frame: &[u8]) -> Result<String> {
    anyhow::ensure!(frame.len() >= 4, "frame has no four-byte length header");
    let length = u32::from_be_bytes(frame[..4].try_into().expect("slice is four bytes")) as usize;
    anyhow::ensure!(length <= MAX_FRAME, "compressed frame is too large");
    anyhow::ensure!(
        frame.len() == 4 + length,
        "frame length does not match header"
    );

    let mut decoder = GzDecoder::new(&frame[4..]);
    let mut plain = Vec::new();
    decoder
        .by_ref()
        .take((MAX_FRAME + 1) as u64)
        .read_to_end(&mut plain)
        .context("invalid gzip payload")?;
    anyhow::ensure!(plain.len() <= MAX_FRAME, "decompressed WML is too large");
    String::from_utf8(plain).context("WML payload is not UTF-8")
}

pub fn read_frame(reader: &mut impl Read) -> io::Result<Vec<u8>> {
    let mut header = [0_u8; 4];
    reader.read_exact(&mut header)?;
    let length = u32::from_be_bytes(header) as usize;
    if length > MAX_FRAME {
        return Err(io::Error::new(
            io::ErrorKind::InvalidData,
            "frame is too large",
        ));
    }
    let mut frame = Vec::with_capacity(4 + length);
    frame.extend_from_slice(&header);
    frame.resize(4 + length, 0);
    reader.read_exact(&mut frame[4..])?;
    Ok(frame)
}

pub fn send_wml(writer: &mut impl Write, wml: &str) -> Result<()> {
    let frame = encode_frame(wml)?;
    writer
        .write_all(&frame)
        .context("could not send complete frame")?;
    writer.flush().context("could not flush frame")?;
    Ok(())
}

pub fn encode_chat(sender: &str, message: &str) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {
    let sender = simple_field(sender)?;
    let message = simple_field(message)?;
    encode_frame(&format!(
        "[message]\nmessage=\"{message}\"\nroom=\"lobby\"\nsender=\"{sender}\"\n[/message]"
    ))
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::{decode_frame, encode_chat, encode_frame};

    #[test]
    fn real_chat_shape_round_trips() {
        let frame = encode_chat("ChatBot", "Hello!").unwrap();
        assert_eq!(&frame[4..6], &[0x1F, 0x8B]);
        let plain = decode_frame(&frame).unwrap();
        assert!(plain.contains("message=\"Hello!\""));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_trailing_bytes() {
        let mut frame = encode_frame("[version]\n[/version]").unwrap();
        frame.push(0);
        assert!(decode_frame(&frame).is_err());
    }
}

Read the module by responsibility

Section titled “Read the module by responsibility”

Start with the pure functions that accept and return byte vectors; they are easiest to test. Next read the exact stream functions that repeatedly call read_exact for a header and payload. Finally read send_wml, which owns the complete serialization-and-write transaction.

This order keeps three kinds of failure distinct:

  • transport failure: the socket closed or timed out;
  • framing failure: the advertised message length was impossible;
  • content failure: gzip, UTF-8, or WML data was invalid.

Preserving those categories in error messages is part of the explanation. If everything becomes “chat failed,” a learner cannot tell whether to inspect Wireshark, the frame cursor, or the message serializer.

This interactive lab needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it still explains the same idea.

Lesson 9.5

Protocol State Machines and Replay

A packet parser is only the first layer

Section titled “A packet parser is only the first layer”

Parsing one message tells you what its bytes mean. A protocol also defines when that message is legal.

TL;DR: Valid bytes can still request a transition that makes no sense in the current session.

A local Wesnoth test client might move through:

A chat message before the greeting may be invalid even when its length and UTF-8 text parse perfectly. That makes protocol reversing a state-machine problem as well as a byte-parsing problem.

Replay processes the saved frames in order. A record changes the modeled session only after both its bytes and its transition have passed validation:

If any stage fails, the record and old state remain available for diagnosis; the replay never needs to invent a replacement state.

A message log and a session state are different things

Section titled “A message log and a session state are different things”

The capture is an ordered log of the frames that crossed the connection. The session state is a model produced by applying their messages in order:

For a five-frame capture of one short session, starting from Connected:

Keep the raw log immutable and rebuild the model from it. If a parser or transition rule changes, you can replay the same log and see exactly which frame now produces a different result. Editing the stored “current state” by hand loses that history.

Alternative: Think of the log as receipts and the session state as the current balance. Replay rebuilds the balance from those receipts.

Not every message is an event that happened exactly once. A snapshot can repeat a whole state, while an acknowledgment refers to an earlier request. A retransmitted request may appear twice. Store direction, sequence identifiers, and timing with each frame; without them, duplicate bytes cannot be told apart from duplicate actions. The real-time section below works through those identifiers in detail.

Model states and messages separately

Section titled “Model states and messages separately”

Receiving a well-formed Chat message is different from being ready to accept it. A connection begins in Connected, reaches a lobby only after greeting and room messages, and can then accept chat. These enums keep the connection state and the parsed message as separate facts:

The parser creates Message values. The session machine decides whether each value makes sense now.

Make transitions explicit

Section titled “Make transitions explicit”

Now pair the current state with one parsed message. A version-1 greeting moves Connected to Greeted; an unsupported version returns a precise error; a chat message in the lobby leaves the state unchanged. The match below makes every accepted transition visible in one place:

Drawn as a diagram, apply is this state machine:

Each arrow is one arm of the match. A message with no arrow out of the current state, such as Chat while Greeted, falls through to the last arm and returns IllegalTransition. A Greeting with any version other than 1 is refused by its own arm with UnsupportedVersion, and Goodbye is accepted in every state, including Closed itself.

This is longer than a chain of if statements, but every state and message variant has an explicit case. Adding a variant makes an exhaustive match stop compiling until you decide how to handle it.

Unchanged bytes can be invalid in a new session phase. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

state = Connected
read the next recorded event
check which events are allowed in this state
update state for an accepted transition
deliver Chat only from InLobby
report the stopping phase

Result: Closed, 1 delivered chat event(s), sequence accepted. Replaying bytes does not recreate their original session context.

Final values: order = normal; event = Goodbye; state = Closed; delivered = 1; accepted = true.

Store captures as direction plus bytes

Section titled “Store captures as direction plus bytes”

Do not save only the decoded text. A replay fixture should preserve:

  • client-to-server or server-to-client direction;
  • time relative to the previous frame;
  • exact frame bytes;
  • the game and protocol version;
  • the experiment that produced the capture.

Redact account names or chat content before committing fixtures. A local test capture should contain only invented data.

Replay without a network

Section titled “Replay without a network”

Replay takes recorded frames and the parser used for this protocol version. It starts from Connected, validates each frame’s size and delay, parses its bytes, and applies the resulting message to the session state. The returned state is the result of those messages under the current transition function; the error names the frame where interpretation stopped:

The test does not sleep for after_ms. It validates timing metadata deterministically. A separate integration test can use a virtual clock to exercise timeouts.

Deterministic replay requires controlling every input that affects a transition: message order, clock readings, random choices, configuration, and initial state. If the same fixture sometimes reaches different states, one of those inputs is still hidden. Pass it into the model instead of reading a real clock or global setting from inside apply.

For example, imagine a lobby rule that closes a connection if no greeting arrives within five seconds. The same captured Greeting should be accepted at 4,900 ms and rejected at 5,100 ms when a test supplies those times to a virtual clock. Reading the wall clock inside apply would make the result depend on how fast the test machine runs. The small replay function above only checks that after_ms is plausible; a timeout test needs a clock-aware version of the model. The same rule applies when testing cooldowns or turn timers in another game.

Mutate one fact at a time

Section titled “Mutate one fact at a time”

Useful negative replays include:

  • truncate one length prefix;
  • make a length larger than the available payload;
  • send chat before greeting;
  • repeat a one-time greeting;
  • remove the final frame;
  • insert an unknown message type;
  • exceed the maximum accepted text length.

The expected outcome is a precise error at a precise frame, never an out-of-bounds read or an infinite wait. Replaying Greeting twice, for example, stops at frame 1 with an IllegalTransition error for state Greeted, because the state machine has no Greeting arrow out of Greeted.

Narration: A single changed field lets a rejected replay identify one failed assumption instead of several competing explanations.

A length larger than the available payload has to fail before any message is decoded:

For messages that may be retried, test idempotence explicitly. Applying the same acknowledgment twice should either preserve the same state or return a clear duplicate error; it should not create a second match, grant a reward twice, or move backward in the session.

Think of a toy server processing a request claim reward #42. If the reply is lost, the client may send the same request again. The server can remember request #42 and return the earlier result, or reject it as a duplicate; adding five gold again would be a bug. The identifier is what makes “same request” testable. A repeated Chat with identical text could instead be a new message, so matching bytes alone is not a safe duplicate rule.

Why replay beats manual clicking

Section titled “Why replay beats manual clicking”

A capture preserves one session. A replay turns it into a repeatable test: when you change the parser, framing code, or session rules, the same frames run through them again in milliseconds.

Keep live-network code at the edge. Feed the bytes it receives into the same parser and state machine tested by replay. That design keeps transport separate from parsing and makes the protocol model reproducible. 🌐

From session replay to real-time state

Section titled “From session replay to real-time state”

The Wesnoth lobby replay above checked whether each message was legal in one conversation. A fast action game adds a second question: which version of the world should the client draw while messages are still travelling? The same capture, framing, and state-machine discipline applies, but ticks and sequence numbers become part of the state.

Real-time games replicate a simulation, not just variables

Section titled “Real-time games replicate a simulation, not just variables”

Most action games advance the world in discrete ticks. If a server runs at 60 ticks per second, one simulation step is approximately:

The client samples input, labels it, and sends a command. The server processes commands during its own ticks and periodically sends a snapshot or delta. The client then draws frames between confirmed server states:

A field’s meaning depends on the kind of message carrying it. Imagine a player at (10, 15) requesting a move north to (10, 14). The request is an intent; the coordinate is a desired destination. An acknowledgment confirms that a command arrived or was applied. A snapshot reports enough state to stand alone, while a delta reports only changes from an identified earlier state. If the server replies with (10, 14), that coordinate is an accepted position. Equal-looking bytes can have different authority.

Several similar-looking states can therefore coexist:

State Purpose Important label
Last confirmed state What the server has accepted Server tick or snapshot ID
Predicted state Immediate response to local input Last locally simulated command
Interpolated state Smooth display of remote objects Render timestamp between snapshots
Historical state Rewind or lag-compensation query Past server tick or time

This explains why a coordinate found in memory can be correct yet appear to “snap back.” You may have found the predicted or rendered copy while a later server snapshot replaced it. Three facts tell the copies apart: which thread writes the field, whether its updates follow input or incoming packets, and which tick or sequence number travels beside it.

Ordering has to be carried in the message

Section titled “Ordering has to be carried in the message”

Packet arrival order is not automatically simulation order. UDP packets can arrive late or twice; even over TCP, one stream can contain application events whose own timestamps refer to different moments. Protocols commonly carry:

  • a monotonically increasing sequence number;
  • a server tick or timestamp;
  • an acknowledgment of the newest processed command;
  • a bit mask acknowledging several earlier packets;
  • a baseline ID telling which snapshot a delta modifies.

Sequence numbers often wrap. For an unsigned N-bit counter, comparisons must use modular arithmetic and accept only a bounded forward window, not a plain incoming > current test.

Work through one 16-bit wraparound. The last accepted sequence number is 65534, and the next two packets carry 65535 and then 0:

The naive test gets the first packet right and the second one wrong. 0 really is one step newer than 65535, but as a plain integer it is smaller, so the packet is thrown away. It gets worse from there: current never advances past 65535, so every sequence number after the wrap looks old in the same way, and the connection appears to stop receiving updates entirely.

The modular test asks a different question — how far forward is incoming from current, counting the wrap? (0 - 65535) mod 65536 is 1, a single step ahead, so the packet is accepted and current moves on. Accept only while that distance stays inside an agreed window such as 1..=32767. A distance of 32768 is exactly halfway around a 16-bit counter and cannot be classified as newer or older from the sequence number alone, so this rule refuses it. A genuinely old packet computes a distance near 65536, which also falls outside the window. The exact window is part of the protocol contract and deserves boundary tests; RFC 1982’s serial-number arithmetic explains the half-range limit.

A snapshot contains enough state to stand alone. A delta contains changes relative to a named baseline. Applying a delta to the wrong baseline may parse perfectly and still create nonsense. Robust tooling keeps the baseline ID with the bytes, refuses missing dependencies, and bounds how long incomplete state may wait.

The live bot in Lesson 9.6 returns to the simpler Wesnoth lobby conversation. It uses the same separation between framed bytes, decoded messages, and legal session actions that replay made visible.

Lesson 9.6

Clients, Handshakes, and Chat Automation

What we are building

Section titled “What we are building”

Run wesnothd.exe on your own computer, connect a client named ChatBot, and make it answer \wave with Hello! in the lobby.

This is not a toy protocol. It uses the exact flow we reversed from Wesnoth 1.14.9:

Keep transport, decoding, session meaning, and behavior as separate layers. One incoming message should travel through the pipeline before any reply is built:

A parsed message still needs session context. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

read the selected inputs
evaluate each stated condition
combine the required conditions
perform the effect only when accepted
otherwise retain the old state
report the result and its limits

Result: one greeting reply is prepared for serialization, compression and framing.

Final values: phase = lobby; message = wave; in_lobby = true; text_matches = true; accepted = true; reply = Hello! from ChatBot.

This separation lets a malformed frame fail before it reaches chat behavior, and it lets the command handler work with events instead of raw network bytes.

Connect with timeouts

Section titled “Connect with timeouts”

Before reading protocol bytes, the client needs a connection that cannot silently drift to another host or wait forever for a stalled local server. connect_local accepts one socket address, checks that it is the course loopback endpoint, then sets finite connect, read, and write waits:

TL;DR: A timeout bounds how long the bot can wait; a verified endpoint bounds whom it talks to.

The timeout prevents a broken server or parser from hanging the bot forever.

Read and write exact frames

Section titled “Read and write exact frames”

Lesson 9.4’s encode_wesnoth_frame performs the gzip compression and adds the four-byte big-endian length. write_all matters because one write may send only part of a buffer.

The two helpers implement the strip in opposite directions. send_wml frames text and writes all bytes; read_frame reads the four-byte length, checks the cap, then reads that many payload bytes before a decoder sees them. A short TCP read is normal, so both paths use the exact-read/write operations:

read_exact handles TCP fragmentation. It does not assume one receive call equals one Wesnoth message.

Handle early server replies

Section titled “Handle early server replies”

The opening negotiation is special, so collect its replies until a short quiet period. The historical capture received 41 bytes.

Alternative: Treat the connection like a conversation: inspect the reply before deciding which question is appropriate next.

This quiet-period reader is only for the unframed negotiation reply. It collects successive TCP reads until the server closes or pauses briefly, while the size cap prevents an unexpected reply from growing forever. After login, read_frame uses the protocol’s length field instead:

Keep this helper for negotiation only. Once the session is in the lobby, use the frame reader.

Perform the Wesnoth 1.14.9 login

Section titled “Perform the Wesnoth 1.14.9 login”
Windows VM

The parser and frame writer now have a concrete job. The course server first expects four zero negotiation bytes, then a version message and a login message in compressed WML frames. log_in sends them in that order and reads each reply before advancing; a nickname is validated before it enters WML:

If the server rejects the version, compare the decompressed frame with the one produced by the official 1.14.9 client. Do not randomly change compressed bytes; fix the WML and recompress it.

Answer \wave

Section titled “Answer \wave”

Once the login succeeds, the client announces itself and loops over framed server messages. A decoded \wave event will produce the reply described above; ordinary messages leave the connection running:

Prove the bot works

Section titled “Prove the bot works”
  1. Start wesnothd.exe.
  2. Run the client with address 127.0.0.1:15000 and nickname ChatBot.
  3. Join localhost:15000 from the normal Wesnoth client.
  4. Type \wave in the lobby.
  5. Confirm Hello! appears from ChatBot.

That visible lobby response proves the real negotiation, version, login, gzip framing, Simple WML, receive loop, and command logic all work together.

Keep it well behaved

Section titled “Keep it well behaved”

Limit message length, respond at most once per command frame, add a short send rate limit, and exit cleanly when the local server closes. A parser error should print the frame size and stop; it should not enter an automatic reconnect storm.

Narration: A reply rate limit prevents one repeated command from filling the lobby with messages.

Run the complete bot

Section titled “Run the complete bot”

After building the workspace, start the course wesnothd.exe on port 15000 and run:

The full client is wesnoth_chatbot.rs. The framing/parser it imports is wesnoth_protocol.rs. Together they implement the real loopback connection, timeouts, four-zero negotiation, version frame, login frame, lobby receive loop, \wave recognition, and Hello! reply.
