View on GitHub ↗

The reusable gzip/WML framing stays in one tested protocol module; this file owns the session state. That split is intentional: byte framing should not know what \wave means, and chat behavior should not reimplement gzip.

This bot owns its own server connection. Lesson 9.7 puts a relay between the official client and the same local server, so we can observe an existing conversation before choosing one bounded change.

Lesson 9.7

Local Proxies and Bidirectional Streams

What a proxy does

Section titled “What a proxy does”

A local TCP proxy accepts a client connection, opens a connection to your local server, and relays bytes both ways.

TL;DR: A relay preserves both directions of the conversation while providing a place to observe their bytes.

Begin as a transparent relay. If the protocol fails before you modify anything, fix the relay first. This first version treats bytes as bytes. Only after it passes the normal Wesnoth login should the proxy switch to the framed, message-aware upstream path below. The two modes have different failure behavior: a transparent relay does not need to decode; a message-aware relay must decide what to do when decoding fails.

Restrict both endpoints

Section titled “Restrict both endpoints”

A proxy is easy to connect to the wrong service if an address is copied from a different test. Validate both endpoints as loopback addresses before opening either connection; this helper returns the accepted address so the caller cannot forget which one passed the check:

This course proxy is intentionally not a general remote interception tool.

This board needs JavaScript to move things around. Here is the lesson’s sorting:

Accepted
  • 127.0.0.1:15000 (the local Wesnoth server). 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback address, so this endpoint stays on the same computer.
  • 127.0.0.1:27015 (the proxy’s own address). Same loopback address. The check looks at the IP address, not the port.
  • [::1]:15000 (IPv6 localhost). The check accepts the IPv6 localhost address too, so this one passes as well.
Refused with an error
  • 192.168.1.20:15000 (another computer on the network). It is not loopback. This proxy is intentionally not a general remote interception tool, so the check refuses before opening any connection.
  • 8.8.8.8:15000 (a public internet address). Not loopback, so it is refused before anything connects.
  • 0.0.0.0:27015 (every network interface). The code compares with the localhost addresses exactly, and 0.0.0.0 is not one of them, so it is refused.

Relay one direction

Section titled “Relay one direction”

The standard library can copy a stream until EOF:

TCP is full duplex, so run two relays:

For many connections, an async runtime such as Tokio scales better. Threads keep the first lab easy to see.

Half-closes matter

Section titled “Half-closes matter”

One direction can reach EOF while the other still has data to send. A reliable local Wesnoth proxy should use shutdown(Write) on the destination after that relay finishes, then let the server-to-client relay deliver any remaining game messages before both sockets close.

Alternative: One side can stop speaking while still listening. Closing both directions immediately discards that distinction.

Log metadata, not unlimited payloads

Section titled “Log metadata, not unlimited payloads”

Useful bounded log lines include:

If you parse frame previews, cap their length and avoid logging secrets or full chat histories by default.

Diagnose handshake failures

Section titled “Diagnose handshake failures”

When a transparent proxy fails, compare direct and proxied captures:

  • Did both directions start?
  • Were bytes changed or dropped?
  • Did the client send the server’s port or address inside the protocol?
  • Is there TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption behind HTTPS) or a certificate bound to a hostname?
  • Did a relay block because it waited for EOF?
  • Did one side expect a UDP companion channel?

Do not bypass certificate validation. For encrypted protocols, create a development configuration with certificates you control.

Parse without changing

Section titled “Parse without changing”

The safest next step is a tee:

Keep parsing off the relay’s critical path. If the parser cannot keep up, drop log entries rather than blocking the connection. This tee is for observation. It cannot decide where to insert a new message, because a TCP read does not identify a frame boundary. The insertion path therefore waits for a complete bounded frame and handles parse errors explicitly.

Narration: Observing first provides a baseline: later edits can be compared against traffic that the relay already handled correctly.

Inject a real local Wesnoth chat response

Section titled “Inject a real local Wesnoth chat response”

The original lab used proxy port 27015 and server port 15000. Start wesnothd.exe, start the local proxy, then tell Wesnoth to connect to localhost:27015. Reaching the normal lobby through the proxy proves both directions work.

For injection, one task must own the upstream writer so two threads cannot interleave bytes. After the special four-zero negotiation has passed, have the client-to-server path read one complete Wesnoth frame at a time. Forward the original bytes unchanged, but inspect a decoded copy:

Keep the server-to-client direction as an ordinary transparent relay. The handshake needs one small state flag because its first four zero bytes are not a gzip frame; forward those four bytes directly before switching the upstream parser into framed mode.

The contains check is enough only for this controlled one-command fixture. It could match that text inside an unrelated WML field. A general proxy should parse the WML tree from Lesson 9.4 and inspect the actual chat-message field and session state before inserting a response. The complete lab below uses the same narrow shortcut, so do not treat it as a general message router.

Now send \wave from the real Wesnoth client. The server receives both the original command and the injected Hello! message on the already authenticated connection. This is the practical advantage of the proxy: the official client performs its own login while the proxy observes and modifies the loopback traffic.

Verify the proxy

Section titled “Verify the proxy”

The local proxy is correct when:

  • direct and proxied sessions behave the same;
  • byte counts agree with a packet capture;
  • either side closing ends the session cleanly;
  • an undecodable frame in the message-aware mode returns a clear error before that frame is forwarded; proxy_pair then shuts down both sockets before waiting for the reverse relay. A separate transparent mode could relay bytes without decoding them;
  • non-loopback endpoints are rejected;
  • the only modification is the documented \wave response;
  • removing both decoding and injection returns the proxy to byte-for-byte transparent behavior.

Run the complete proxy

Section titled “Run the complete proxy”
Windows VM

Start wesnothd.exe on its normal local port, then run:

Connect the official Wesnoth 1.14.9 client to localhost:27015. Type \wave after login and confirm the injected Hello! appears. The complete two-direction relay is wesnoth_proxy.rs. It binds only to loopback, forwards the unframed negotiation, parses bounded upstream frames, preserves each original frame, injects through the single upstream writer, half-closes both directions, and keeps the server-to-client stream transparent.

Complete lab source: wesnoth_proxy.rs

wesnoth_proxy.rs

windows-labs/src/bin/ · Rust, 94 lines

View on GitHub ↗

Show the codeHide the code
use std::{
    io::{self, Read, Write},
    net::{IpAddr, Ipv4Addr, Shutdown, SocketAddr, TcpListener, TcpStream},
    thread,
    time::Duration,
};

use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use gha_windows_labs::wesnoth_protocol::{decode_frame, encode_chat, read_frame};

fn loopback(port: u16) -> SocketAddr {
    SocketAddr::new(IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::LOCALHOST), port)
}

fn upstream(mut client: TcpStream, mut server: TcpStream) -> Result<()> {
    // The negotiation request is the protocol's one unframed client message.
    let mut negotiation = [0_u8; 4];
    client.read_exact(&mut negotiation)?;
    anyhow::ensure!(negotiation == [0, 0, 0, 0], "unexpected negotiation bytes");
    server.write_all(&negotiation)?;
    server.flush()?;

    loop {
        let frame = match read_frame(&mut client) {
            Ok(frame) => frame,
            Err(error) if error.kind() == io::ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof => break,
            Err(error) => return Err(error.into()),
        };
        let decoded = decode_frame(&frame)?;
        server.write_all(&frame)?;
        if decoded.contains("message=\"\\wave\"") {
            server.write_all(&encode_chat("ChatBot", "Hello!")?)?;
        }
        server.flush()?;
    }
    server.shutdown(Shutdown::Write)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn downstream(mut server: TcpStream, mut client: TcpStream) -> Result<()> {
    io::copy(&mut server, &mut client)?;
    client.shutdown(Shutdown::Write)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn proxy_pair(client: TcpStream) -> Result<()> {
    let server = TcpStream::connect_timeout(&loopback(15_000), Duration::from_secs(3))
        .context("start local wesnothd.exe on port 15000 first")?;
    client.set_read_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))?;
    client.set_write_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(5)))?;
    server.set_read_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))?;
    server.set_write_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(5)))?;

    // Keep control handles so a decoding failure in the upstream worker can
    // close both directions before we wait for the downstream worker.
    let client_control = client.try_clone()?;
    let server_control = server.try_clone()?;
    let upstream_client = client.try_clone()?;
    let downstream_server = server.try_clone()?;
    let up = thread::spawn(move || upstream(upstream_client, server));
    let down = thread::spawn(move || downstream(downstream_server, client));
    let upstream_result = up
        .join()
        .map_err(|_| anyhow::anyhow!("upstream thread panicked"))
        .and_then(|result| result);
    if upstream_result.is_err() {
        let _ = client_control.shutdown(Shutdown::Both);
        let _ = server_control.shutdown(Shutdown::Both);
    }
    let downstream_result = down
        .join()
        .map_err(|_| anyhow::anyhow!("downstream thread panicked"))
        .and_then(|result| result);
    upstream_result?;
    downstream_result?;
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind(loopback(27_015))?;
    println!("Wesnoth proxy listening on 127.0.0.1:27015 -> 127.0.0.1:15000");
    println!("Connect the official 1.14.9 client to localhost:27015.");
    for connection in listener.incoming() {
        let client = connection?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            client.peer_addr()?.ip().is_loopback(),
            "client is not loopback"
        );
        if let Err(error) = proxy_pair(client) {
            eprintln!("session ended: {error:#}");
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

Only the upstream task writes to the server. That single-writer rule prevents the original frame and injected frame from being interleaved. The downstream task stays byte-for-byte transparent, so one experimental hook cannot accidentally rewrite both directions.

The proxy needs TCP because its two endpoints are network clients. When two cooperating programs run on the same computer, they can exchange the same kind of bounded message through shared memory or a named pipe instead. Lessons 9.8 and 9.9 compare those local transports.

Lesson 9.8

Shared Memory Between Processes

Processes normally have separate address spaces

Section titled “Processes normally have separate address spaces”

The proxy copied messages between sockets. A supported game add-on and a separate visualizer could instead agree on a local shared byte region. The message still needs a layout and a lifetime; only the transport changes.

Two running programs can both use the address 0x00400000, yet those numbers can refer to completely different physical storage. Each process has its own virtual address space.

That separation is a safety feature. A map helper should not need to patch a game process merely to receive a supported event from a mod. Windows provides interprocess communication, or IPC, for programs that intentionally cooperate.

Named shared memory is one IPC option:

The two views do not need the same virtual address. Windows connects both views to the same file-mapping object.

The programs share bytes through one kernel-managed object, not pointers to each other’s private address spaces:

The views may have different addresses, but they expose the same mapped bytes. The small protocol is what turns those bytes back into a trustworthy value.

A mapping object is not the view

Section titled “A mapping object is not the view”

These terms describe different resources:

  • A file-mapping object tells Windows what storage is shared, how large it is, and which protections are allowed.
  • A view maps some or all of that object into one process’s virtual address space.
  • A handle names the mapping object.
  • A pointer from MapViewOfFile names the beginning of one process’s view.

Closing the handle and unmapping the view are separate cleanup operations. The lab uses OwnedHandle for the first and a small MappedView type with Drop for the second.

TL;DR: The handle names the shared mapping; the view is the address where this process can access its bytes.

Paging-file-backed means no ordinary file is required

Section titled “Paging-file-backed means no ordinary file is required”

CreateFileMappingW normally accepts a file handle. Passing INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE asks Windows for storage backed by the system paging file instead. We must provide a nonzero maximum size—in this lab, 4096 bytes.

The name starts with Local\, so it lives in the current logon session’s local namespace. We do not use Global\, which can require extra privilege and makes the scope wider than this lab needs.

Bytes need a tiny protocol

Section titled “Bytes need a tiny protocol”

Memory has no built-in String type. Both programs must agree on a layout:

The four-byte length makes embedded zero bytes unambiguous and lets the reader reject impossible sizes before creating a string slice.

Alternative: Sharing storage is like sharing a notebook: agree on the page layout and on when a complete entry may be read.

This is the beginning of serialization: turning structured information into an agreed byte representation.

The original reader treats the first zero byte as the end of UTF-8 text. A legitimate embedded zero therefore shortens the message. The improved format uses the four-byte length header shown above; the writer must use that same format too.

Validate that a complete header exists before slicing, then check its declared length against the remaining mapping. The length describes payload bytes, not the mapping’s zero padding.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: agree on an explicit length format at both ends, and validate the header before trusting it.

One hazard is worth naming here, even though this one-shot lab sidesteps it by writing only once. Shared memory gives two processes access to the same bytes. It gives them no agreement about when. Nothing prevents a reader from arriving in the middle of a write:

The reader’s length check passes, the UTF-8 decode very likely succeeds, and the text returned is simply wrong — or is half of the previous message. Writing the payload before the length narrows that window without closing it, since the CPU and the compiler may reorder the two stores anyway. Closing it takes a sequence number the reader checks before and after copying, or a real synchronization object.

For a small concrete case, suppose the old payload is READY (five bytes) and the writer announces a new seven-byte payload RUNNING before copying it. The reader can observe length 7 alongside READY and two old padding bytes. Seven bytes fit inside the mapping, and zero bytes are valid UTF-8, so both checks in read_text can succeed while the message is not the one the writer meant to publish. The sequence diagram shows that exact gap between publishing the length and finishing the payload. A shared map is like a notice board both programs can see; visibility does not give either program an agreed moment to read a completed notice.

A wake-up does not protect a shared record. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

record = {health: 100, gold: 80}
reader attempts to copy health
writer updates health and gold together
reader attempts to copy gold
release the shared mutex if used
publish only the copied observation

Result: copied health 100 and gold 80 belong to the same protected record.

Final values: coordination = mutex; copied_health = 100; copied_gold = 80; consistent = true.

Build the writer and reader

Section titled “Build the writer and reader”

Show the codeHide the code
#[cfg(windows)]
mod app {
    use std::{io, slice};

    use anyhow::{Context, ensure};
    use gha_windows_labs::OwnedHandle;
    use windows::{
        Win32::{
            Foundation::INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE,
            System::Memory::{
                CreateFileMappingW, FILE_MAP, FILE_MAP_READ, FILE_MAP_WRITE,
                MEMORY_MAPPED_VIEW_ADDRESS, MapViewOfFile, OpenFileMappingW, PAGE_READWRITE,
                UnmapViewOfFile,
            },
        },
        core::w,
    };

    const MAPPING_BYTES: usize = 4_096;
    const HEADER_BYTES: usize = 4;

    struct MappedView {
        address: MEMORY_MAPPED_VIEW_ADDRESS,
        length: usize,
    }

    impl MappedView {
        fn new(handle: &OwnedHandle, access: FILE_MAP) -> windows::core::Result<Self> {
            // SAFETY: handle refers to a file-mapping object. A null address is
            // checked before any slice is created, and the view is unmapped in Drop.
            let address = unsafe { MapViewOfFile(handle.raw(), access, 0, 0, MAPPING_BYTES) };
            if address.Value.is_null() {
                return Err(windows::core::Error::from_thread());
            }
            Ok(Self {
                address,
                length: MAPPING_BYTES,
            })
        }

        fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
            // SAFETY: MapViewOfFile returned a non-null view of length MAPPING_BYTES,
            // and self keeps the view mapped for the slice's entire lifetime.
            unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts(self.address.Value.cast(), self.length) }
        }

        fn bytes_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
            // SAFETY: the writer requested FILE_MAP_WRITE, owns this mutable borrow,
            // and the mapped range remains valid until Drop.
            unsafe { slice::from_raw_parts_mut(self.address.Value.cast(), self.length) }
        }
    }

    impl Drop for MappedView {
        fn drop(&mut self) {
            // SAFETY: this object owns one live mapped view and unmaps it once.
            let _ = unsafe { UnmapViewOfFile(self.address) };
        }
    }

    fn writer(message: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        ensure!(
            message.len() <= MAPPING_BYTES - HEADER_BYTES,
            "message is longer than {} UTF-8 bytes",
            MAPPING_BYTES - HEADER_BYTES
        );
        // SAFETY: INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE requests paging-file-backed memory. The
        // mapping name is static and the size is nonzero.
        let mapping = unsafe {
            CreateFileMappingW(
                INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE,
                None,
                PAGE_READWRITE,
                0,
                MAPPING_BYTES as u32,
                w!("Local\\GhaSharedMemoryV1"),
            )
        }?;
        let mapping = OwnedHandle::from_raw(mapping)?;
        let mut view = MappedView::new(&mapping, FILE_MAP_WRITE)?;
        let bytes = view.bytes_mut();
        bytes.fill(0);
        bytes[..HEADER_BYTES].copy_from_slice(&(message.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
        bytes[HEADER_BYTES..HEADER_BYTES + message.len()].copy_from_slice(message.as_bytes());

        println!(
            "Published {} UTF-8 bytes to a Local\\ mapping.",
            message.len()
        );
        println!("Run `shared_memory_lab read` in another window.");
        println!("Press Enter here after the reader finishes.");
        let mut line = String::new();
        io::stdin().read_line(&mut line)?;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn reader() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // SAFETY: the name is static, inheritance is disabled, and the reader
        // requests read-only access.
        let mapping = unsafe {
            OpenFileMappingW(
                FILE_MAP_READ.0,
                false,
                w!("Local\\GhaSharedMemoryV1"),
            )
        }
        .context("open the writer first so the named mapping exists")?;
        let mapping = OwnedHandle::from_raw(mapping)?;
        let view = MappedView::new(&mapping, FILE_MAP_READ)?;
        let bytes = view.bytes();
        let length = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[..HEADER_BYTES].try_into()?) as usize;
        ensure!(
            length <= MAPPING_BYTES - HEADER_BYTES,
            "shared-memory length header is out of range"
        );
        let message = std::str::from_utf8(&bytes[HEADER_BYTES..HEADER_BYTES + length])
            .context("shared message was not valid UTF-8")?;
        println!("Read {length} bytes: {message}");
        println!("The reader requested FILE_MAP_READ and changed nothing.");
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn run() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let mut arguments = std::env::args().skip(1);
        match arguments.next().as_deref() {
            Some("write") => {
                let message = arguments.collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ");
                let message = if message.is_empty() {
                    "Wesnoth turn 12: local lab ready"
                } else {
                    &message
                };
                writer(message)
            }
            Some("read") => reader(),
            _ => anyhow::bail!("usage: shared_memory_lab write <message> | shared_memory_lab read"),
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(windows)]
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    app::run()
}

#[cfg(not(windows))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("This named shared-memory lab must run on Windows.");
}

Why is this unsafe code contained?

Section titled “Why is this unsafe code contained?”

MapViewOfFile returns a raw pointer. The compiler cannot prove how many bytes it covers, whether the view is writable, or when Windows unmaps it. MappedView establishes those facts once, then ordinary methods return bounded slices.

The writer receives &mut [u8]; the reader receives &[u8]. That is semantic highlighting at the type-system level: mutability shows which side is allowed to change data.

Run two copies

Section titled “Run two copies”
Windows VM

In PowerShell window one:

Leave it waiting. In window two:

Return to window one and press Enter. The mapping object disappears after the last handle closes, so another reader should then receive a clear “open the writer first” error.

Narration: Both the reader and writer must take the same mutex; signalling an event does not exclude a partial read.

Where shared memory fits

Section titled “Where shared memory fits”

A Wesnoth add-on or game build could publish a tiny turn/event record. A separate visualizer could read it. The producer defines the shared-memory contract, so both sides agree on its layout and lifetime.

The one-shot lab avoids concurrent writes. A concurrent design could hold the same named mutex while the writer updates a record and while the reader copies it; the reader would then avoid mixing old and new fields. Both sides also need a shared format version and an agreed sequence-number meaning. A notification event alone announces readiness; it does not by itself protect the copy. Never put passwords or secret tokens in a mapping protected only by a convenient name.

The buildable source is shared_memory_lab.rs.

References: sharing files and memory, creating named shared memory, CreateFileMappingW, and MapViewOfFile.

Lesson 9.9 uses a named pipe when the producer and consumer would rather exchange one request and one reply than coordinate reads of a shared region.

Lesson 9.9

Named Pipes and Local Message Framing

A named pipe is a local client/server channel

Section titled “A named pipe is a local client/server channel”

Shared memory in Lesson 9.8 gave two programs views of the same bytes, but a concurrent writer needed an additional timing agreement. For one request followed by one reply, a named pipe gives us a connection with an explicit read/write order.

A named pipe server creates a known pipe name and waits. A client opens that name. After they connect, both sides can exchange bytes through ordinary Windows read and write calls.

This resembles a tiny network service, but the lab keeps both programs on the same Windows machine:

Named pipes are useful when a supported game plug-in, launcher, capture helper, or your own engine build needs to talk to a separate tool without sharing raw pointers.

One bounded exchange has a clear beginning, two validated messages, and a clear end:

The pipe transports bytes. Both programs still need to agree on the length field, message kinds, payload encoding, and which requests to reject.

Note

🔌 IPC idea: define a small message format instead of sharing addresses. Each process keeps ownership of its own memory and exchanges bounded copies.

Message mode preserves write boundaries

Section titled “Message mode preserves write boundaries”

Windows pipes can operate in byte mode or message mode.

TL;DR: Message mode remembers write boundaries, but a small read buffer can still return only part of one message.

  • Byte mode is a stream. One read can receive part of a write or data from several writes.
  • Message mode preserves message boundaries. A read receives one message, provided the buffer is large enough.

The lab selects PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE when creating the server and PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE for both ends.

It still adds a four-byte length header. Why use both? Message mode keeps transport boundaries, while the length header validates the application protocol. The receiver can reject a damaged or unexpected frame instead of trusting every byte Windows delivered.

Treat IPC data like untrusted input

Section titled “Treat IPC data like untrusted input”

“Local” does not mean “automatically trustworthy.” Another program in the same account or session might know or guess the pipe name.

Alternative: A local sender is another program. Validate its lengths and contents just as you would a network sender.

The receiver checks all of these facts before making a String:

  1. At least four header bytes arrived.
  2. The declared text length is no more than 1024 bytes.
  3. The received frame size equals 4 + declared length.
  4. The text bytes are valid UTF-8.

The server accepts one client, handles one request, sends one fixed reply, and exits. Small limits make the behavior easy to reason about.

This byte-stream counterexample shows why a single successful read need not contain a complete payload. The Windows lab below chooses message mode and still checks lengths.

One byte-stream message can arrive in pieces. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

promised_payload_bytes = 8
copied = read(first_fragment)
remaining = promised_payload_bytes - copied
read again until remaining == 0
parse only the complete bounded payload
report read calls and assembled bytes

Result: eight bytes assembled in 2 read call(s). A disconnected or malformed sender must fail instead of inventing missing bytes.

Final values: first = 3; expected = 8; copied = 8; read_calls = 2; remaining = 0; parsed = true.

Keep the pipe local and never impersonate

Section titled “Keep the pipe local and never impersonate”

Named pipes can support remote clients. This lab includes PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, so Windows rejects them automatically.

This original creation helper chooses message mode and duplex access, but does not explicitly reject remote clients. This helper extracts the creation step from the complete lab below, using its pipe name and FRAME_BYTES buffer limit; OwnedHandle closes the created pipe. Accepting and parsing the request happens later.

Add the local-only capability boundary to the creation mode. It rejects remote clients at the Windows pipe boundary; it does not replace the normal access check for local clients.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: restrict who can reach a channel when creating it, then validate each received message.

The program does not call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient, duplicate tokens, start a process as another identity, or change privileges. Those operations solve different identity and access-control problems; they are not part of this message channel.

Build both modes in one program

Section titled “Build both modes in one program”

Show the codeHide the code
#[cfg(windows)]
mod app {
    use anyhow::{Context, ensure};
    use gha_windows_labs::OwnedHandle;
    use windows::{
        Win32::{
            Foundation::{ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED, GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE},
            Storage::FileSystem::{
                CreateFileW, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, FILE_SHARE_MODE, OPEN_EXISTING,
                PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, ReadFile, WriteFile,
            },
            System::Pipes::{
                ConnectNamedPipe, CreateNamedPipeW, PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE,
                PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE, PIPE_WAIT, SetNamedPipeHandleState,
            },
        },
        core::w,
    };

    const MAX_TEXT_BYTES: usize = 1_024;
    const FRAME_BYTES: usize = MAX_TEXT_BYTES + 4;

    fn frame(text: &str) -> anyhow::Result<Vec<u8>> {
        ensure!(
            text.len() <= MAX_TEXT_BYTES,
            "message is longer than {MAX_TEXT_BYTES} UTF-8 bytes"
        );
        let mut bytes = Vec::with_capacity(text.len() + 4);
        bytes.extend_from_slice(&(text.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
        bytes.extend_from_slice(text.as_bytes());
        Ok(bytes)
    }

    fn read_frame(handle: &OwnedHandle) -> anyhow::Result<String> {
        let mut buffer = [0_u8; FRAME_BYTES];
        let mut bytes_read = 0_u32;
        // SAFETY: buffer is writable, bytes_read is a valid output pointer,
        // and this synchronous lab does not supply an OVERLAPPED structure.
        unsafe { ReadFile(handle.raw(), Some(&mut buffer), Some(&mut bytes_read), None) }?;
        let bytes_read = bytes_read as usize;
        ensure!(
            bytes_read >= 4,
            "pipe message did not contain a length header"
        );
        let declared = u32::from_le_bytes(buffer[..4].try_into()?) as usize;
        ensure!(
            declared <= MAX_TEXT_BYTES,
            "pipe length header is too large"
        );
        ensure!(
            bytes_read == declared + 4,
            "pipe frame length did not match its header"
        );
        Ok(std::str::from_utf8(&buffer[4..bytes_read])
            .context("pipe message was not valid UTF-8")?
            .to_owned())
    }

    fn write_frame(handle: &OwnedHandle, text: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let bytes = frame(text)?;
        let mut bytes_written = 0_u32;
        // SAFETY: bytes remains readable during the synchronous call and
        // bytes_written is a valid output pointer.
        unsafe { WriteFile(handle.raw(), Some(&bytes), Some(&mut bytes_written), None) }?;
        ensure!(
            bytes_written as usize == bytes.len(),
            "Windows wrote only part of the pipe frame"
        );
        Ok(())
    }

    fn server() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let mode =
            PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE | PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE | PIPE_WAIT | PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS;
        // SAFETY: the pipe name is static. The server allows one synchronous,
        // message-mode connection and supplies no custom security pointer.
        let pipe = unsafe {
            CreateNamedPipeW(
                w!(r"\\.\pipe\gha-local-game-ipc-v1"),
                PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX,
                mode,
                1,
                FRAME_BYTES as u32,
                FRAME_BYTES as u32,
                0,
                None,
            )
        };
        let pipe = OwnedHandle::from_raw(pipe)?;
        println!("Server is waiting for one local client...");

        // A client can connect between CreateNamedPipeW and ConnectNamedPipe.
        // In that harmless race, Windows reports ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED.
        // SAFETY: pipe owns a valid server-pipe handle and this synchronous
        // call deliberately supplies no OVERLAPPED structure.
        match unsafe { ConnectNamedPipe(pipe.raw(), None) } {
            Ok(()) => {}
            Err(error) if error.code() == ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED.to_hresult() => {}
            Err(error) => return Err(error.into()),
        }

        let message = read_frame(&pipe)?;
        println!("Client said: {message}");
        write_frame(&pipe, "ACK: the local game-tool message arrived")?;
        println!("Replied once; the server will now close the pipe.");
        Ok(())
    }

    fn client(message: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // SAFETY: the path is static. This opens only the local course pipe,
        // requests read/write data access, and does not inherit the handle.
        let pipe = unsafe {
            CreateFileW(
                w!(r"\\.\pipe\gha-local-game-ipc-v1"),
                GENERIC_READ.0 | GENERIC_WRITE.0,
                FILE_SHARE_MODE(0),
                None,
                OPEN_EXISTING,
                FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL,
                None,
            )
        }
        .context("start `named_pipe_lab server` in another window first")?;
        let pipe = OwnedHandle::from_raw(pipe)?;
        let read_mode = PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE;
        // SAFETY: pipe is a connected named-pipe handle and read_mode remains
        // valid for the duration of the call.
        unsafe { SetNamedPipeHandleState(pipe.raw(), Some(&read_mode), None, None) }?;

        write_frame(&pipe, message)?;
        println!("Server replied: {}", read_frame(&pipe)?);
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn run() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let mut arguments = std::env::args().skip(1);
        match arguments.next().as_deref() {
            Some("server") => server(),
            Some("client") => {
                let message = arguments.collect::<Vec<_>>().join(" ");
                let message = if message.is_empty() {
                    "Wesnoth helper connected"
                } else {
                    &message
                };
                client(message)
            }
            _ => anyhow::bail!("usage: named_pipe_lab server | named_pipe_lab client <message>"),
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(windows)]
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    app::run()
}

#[cfg(not(windows))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("This local named-pipe lab must run on Windows.");
}

Understand the connection race

Section titled “Understand the connection race”

A client can open the pipe after CreateNamedPipeW creates it but just before the server calls ConnectNamedPipe. Windows then returns ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED. That does not mean the connection failed—it means the client already won the race.

Narration: A client can connect before the server starts waiting; that successful connection must not be mistaken for a failed session.

The match arm accepts only that documented condition and returns every other error:

The client may connect in the narrow interval before the server calls ConnectNamedPipe. In that case Windows reports ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED, which means the connection already exists rather than that it failed. The match below accepts both successful outcomes and propagates other errors:

Run the request and reply

Section titled “Run the request and reply”
Windows VM

In window one:

In window two:

The client prints the acknowledgement and both programs exit. Start the server again for another message.

How to grow this design safely

Section titled “How to grow this design safely”

A larger tool could add a version number and an enum of allowed messages such as TurnStarted, MapLoaded, or PlayerPositionFromSupportedMod. It should authenticate sensitive clients, set an explicit security descriptor, rate-limit messages, keep bounded queues, and separate parsing from actions.

Do not accept a command string and pass it to PowerShell or cmd.exe. Define a small message enum and reject unknown variants. Data should select one defined action, not become code.

The buildable source is named_pipe_lab.rs.

References: named-pipe operations, CreateNamedPipeW, ConnectNamedPipe, and SetNamedPipeHandleState.

Lesson 9.10

How the Source Engine Works

You press forward. Your player moves immediately, yet the server has not received the input. Later, a reply may adjust that movement. To understand why, follow the input across the pieces of the game that own each decision. Lesson 9.1 introduced client and server messages. Source gives us a concrete engine in which those messages connect to objects and time.

Why study Source?

Section titled “Why study Source?”

Source is Valve’s game-engine family behind Half-Life 2, Counter-Strike: Source, Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead, and the original Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. They share architectural ideas, but their engine branches differ. Counter-Strike 2 uses Source 2, a later engine family. An interface name or memory layout from Source 1 is not a promise about Counter-Strike 2.

Valve’s public Source SDK 2013 supplies game code and interfaces for Half-Life 2, Half-Life 2: Deathmatch, and Team Fortress 2. An SDK, or software development kit, gives developers code and tools for building compatible software. This repository lets us inspect the game side of the boundary. It does not supply every implementation inside a shipping engine.

This lesson follows the SDK revision beginning b8cfb12. Treat its named interfaces and defaults as facts about that revision. Keep experiments in your own offline SDK mod. A mod supplies changed game content or behavior while using the engine’s supported loading contracts.

The engine connects client and server game code

Section titled “The engine connects client and server game code”

A launcher starts the engine and selects the game to load. The engine provides common services such as files, rendering, sound, and networking. Game-specific code defines weapons and entities, calculates movement and damage, and decides how those objects respond to input and contact.

On Windows, this game code commonly comes in client.dll and server.dll. A DLL is a library loaded into a process while it runs, as introduced in Lesson 8.1. Other operating systems use their own shared-library formats for the same architectural division.

The client library handles the player’s input, local presentation, and prediction. The server library calculates movement, collisions, damage, and other changes to the match state; it sends the accepted results to clients. Some movement code is shared so both sides can compute comparable results. Rendering a player and deciding whether that player can pass a wall are separate responsibilities.

A listen server hosts the simulation inside a game that also has a local player. A dedicated server runs the hosting side without that local player’s view. Even a local game can retain the client/server division. The boundary describes who owns a decision, whether its messages cross the Internet or stay on one machine.

TL;DR: The client presents and predicts. The server decides the game state. The engine connects their game libraries.

Modules ask for an interface by name

Section titled “Modules ask for an interface by name”

The engine cannot call an arbitrary function inside a loaded library and hope its arguments fit. The two sides need an agreed set of operations. That set is an interface: a contract describing which methods an object provides and how to call them.

Source modules expose a factory named CreateInterface. A factory is a function that supplies an object through an agreed interface. The caller passes the requested name. The module searches its registered interfaces and returns a pointer to the matching object, or a null pointer if it cannot provide one. An optional status output receives IFACE_OK or IFACE_FAILED. The pointer is the function’s result; the status is a separate output.

For this revision, VClient017 names the client game interface, while VEngineClient014 names engine services used by client code. On the server side, VEngineServer023 exposes engine services, ServerGameDLL012 exposes game callbacks, and ServerGameClients005 covers player-related callbacks. The suffix is part of the requested contract.

The SDK’s registration macros, including EXPOSE_INTERFACE, attach a name and creation function to a registration list. Lookup matches that name. The returned object’s virtual methods use the C++ calling contract already introduced in earlier lessons. A different interface version can change that contract, even when its name looks similar.

Alternative: Picture a shared menu of operations. The version name selects the menu both modules agree to use.

This explains a startup failure that otherwise looks mysterious: a library loads successfully, but it cannot provide the interface the engine asks for. Loading bytes and agreeing on their callable contract are different checks.

Entity state becomes selected network properties

Section titled “Entity state becomes selected network properties”

Once the libraries connect, the server can create an entity, an object the game tracks: a player, door, projectile, or another piece of the world. Its full object contains more information than a client needs. Some fields are server bookkeeping. Others describe what the client must display.

A SendTable declares properties that server game code makes available for network encoding. A corresponding RecvTable describes how client game code receives those properties. These are descriptions of fields and their encoding, rather than a copy of the whole C++ object. Nested tables let one class reuse another class’s networked fields.

Think of a door whose server object stores its position, opening state, and internal scheduling data. The client needs enough state to place and draw the door. It does not need every scheduling field. The property declarations make that selection explicit. The engine can also limit which entities and updates are relevant to a particular client.

Floating-point properties can trade precision for bandwidth through quantization: representing a range with a limited set of codes. As an illustration, four bits give 2⁴ = 16 codes. Spread those codes across a chosen range from 0 to 15, including both ends. The spacing is (15 − 0) ÷ (16 − 1) = 1. Values between the available steps need an encoding rule that chooses a representable value.

The SDK’s SendPropFloat accepts a bit count, range, and flags. Some settings use an unscaled float instead. The four-bit example explains the trade; it does not describe every Source float on the wire. A client-side value can therefore differ slightly from the server’s value even when both sides work correctly.

Input becomes a command record

Section titled “Input becomes a command record”

Now the player presses a movement key. The client game interface’s CreateMove produces a user command, one record of player input for simulation. Source names that record CUserCmd.

Its command_number identifies a command in the sequence. Its tick_count records the tick when the client created it. A tick is one step of the simulation clock. Command numbers and tick numbers have different jobs, even when a small example gives them matching values.

The record includes view angles and the intended movement values forwardmove, sidemove, and upmove. It also includes weapon selection and mouse movement. These inputs describe what the player requests. They do not establish the final position, damage, or inventory result.

The buttons field packs several requests into one integer. In this SDK, attack uses bit 0 and jump uses bit 1. Their values are 2⁰ = 1 and 2¹ = 2. Requesting both sets the combined mask 1 | 2 = 3, whose two lowest bits are on. The server can test each bit separately.

This memory object is not the packet format. Command encoding records changes relative to another command, and decoding rebuilds the record. Fields used for local prediction bookkeeping do not all become raw packet bytes. Keeping object layout and wire encoding separate matters just as it did for the message parsers earlier in this chapter.

A tick advances the world; prediction advances the local estimate

Section titled “A tick advances the world; prediction advances the local estimate”

The SDK’s default tick interval is 0.015 seconds. Multiply by 1000 to get 15 milliseconds per tick. Divide one second by the interval to get 1 ÷ 0.015 ≈ 66.67 simulation steps per second. A game can supply its own interval, so this default is not every Source game’s rate.

The server game interface exposes GameFrame for simulation work and GetTickInterval for its interval. Drawing frames happens on another schedule. A faster renderer can draw additional views between simulation ticks; it does not give the player additional accepted movement.

Waiting for a network reply before showing every step would make movement feel delayed. Prediction lets the client run its local player’s movement using input commands immediately. The server still runs its own simulation and returns authoritative results. Authoritative means that those results are the state the client must reconcile with.

Use a deliberately small movement model to see the reconciliation. Start at x = 0. Each accepted forward command adds one position unit. Commands 1 and 2 request +1, giving 0 + 1 = 1, then 1 + 1 = 2. These are toy displacements, not Source’s velocity and collision formulas. The scene’s 15-millisecond clock comes from the SDK default.

A barrier now closes on the server and prevents movement past x = 2. The client has not received that update. Command 3 requests another +1. The client predicts 2 + 1 = 3; server collision keeps the position at 2. Before the reply arrives, command 4 requests −1. The client’s current prediction becomes 3 − 1 = 2.

Narration: The server’s barrier has closed. The client’s earlier prediction has not heard about it yet.

Acknowledge commands, then replay only the pending ones. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

client predicts all four commands
server executes the acknowledged prefix
receive server position and barrier
drop commands through the acknowledgement
replay the remaining commands from server state
report the corrected predicted position

Result: server snapshot 2, 1 pending command(s), corrected prediction 1. Replaying an already acknowledged command would apply its effect twice.

Final values: ack = 3; barrier = yes; old_prediction = 2; server_position = 2; pending = 1; prediction = 1.

The server reply acknowledges command 3 and reports position 2. An acknowledgment identifies the input already covered by the returned state. The client starts from that authoritative position and drops commands 1 through 3 from its pending history. Command 4 is still pending, so it replays that −1: 2 − 1 = 1.

That replay preserves the player’s newer input while correcting the earlier prediction. Simply replacing the displayed position would lose pending movement. Replaying commands already acknowledged would repeat work the server’s state already contains.

Snapshots smooth other players; lag compensation checks past positions

Section titled “Snapshots smooth other players; lag compensation checks past positions”

A snapshot describes server state at a point in simulation time. It may be encoded as changes from an earlier known snapshot. Snapshot delivery, tick rate, and rendering rate are separate schedules.

For another player’s movement, the client usually has received states rather than that player’s newest input. Interpolation draws intermediate positions between received states. Showing a slightly older timeline gives the renderer states on both sides of the time it wants to draw. That makes motion smooth instead of jumping whenever a message arrives.

Prediction estimates the local player’s response to input. Interpolation fills the visible gaps between other entities’ received states. Neither makes a client observation newer than the information actually received.

This delay also matters when a player fires. The target they saw may occupy an earlier position than the server’s current position. Lag compensation temporarily uses recorded earlier player states for the relevant server-side hit check, then restores the current simulation.

In this SDK, the initial target tick is the command’s tick_count minus the interpolation delay expressed in ticks. The server also checks that time against its latency estimate. A discrepancy greater than 0.2 seconds uses a latency-based target instead. The inspected sv_maxunlag default is 1 second and bounds the allowed correction. This is a bound on the decision; it is not a promise that every past state remains available for exactly one second.

The important ownership stays intact: the server performs the hit check. It temporarily adjusts eligible recorded player state and then restores it. The world does not permanently travel backward because a packet arrived.

Console variables have permissions as well as values

Section titled “Console variables have permissions as well as values”

Games need settings without recompiling each change. A console variable, or ConVar, is a named setting with a value and flags describing how it may be used. The developer console exposes these settings and named commands.

FCVAR_CHEAT restricts certain development controls to permitted cheat contexts, including the server’s sv_cheats setting. FCVAR_REPLICATED marks a server-controlled setting enforced on connected clients. Flags describe permissions and ownership as well as storage behavior.

A server can ask for a client’s variable through StartQueryCvarValue. The request returns a cookie, an identifier for matching a later reply to that request. It does not return the variable’s value immediately. OnQueryCvarValueFinished supplies the later status and value. The FCVAR_SERVER_CANNOT_QUERY flag forbids that query for the marked variable.

For a defender, a client-reported setting is evidence about what the client reported. It does not replace server-side movement, inventory, or damage validation. A timeout or failed query also needs its own interpretation; it is not automatically proof of cheating.

The same engine loads packages and compiled maps

Section titled “The same engine loads packages and compiled maps”

Those entities need geometry, models, textures, and sounds. VPK, short for Valve PacK, bundles resource files behind a directory tree. An entry identifies where its bytes live, possibly in a companion archive. Some bytes can be stored with the directory as preload data. This lets the file system locate a resource without treating every small asset as a separate loose file.

A BSP is a compiled map. The name comes from binary space partitioning, which divides space to organize geometry queries. A Source BSP contains sections called lumps, holding map data such as geometry, visibility, and starting entity definitions. It can also contain embedded resources.

The inspected header starts with VBSP, then a version and a directory of 64 lump descriptors. Each descriptor provides an offset, length, and version-related metadata. Different game branches can interpret sections differently. Reading a file therefore starts with identifying its format and validating its bounded sections, not treating its bytes as a live entity object. Chapter 9 develops that file-validation work.

Use each boundary for the question it can answer

Section titled “Use each boundary for the question it can answer”

An offline observer built with supported interfaces can record command numbers, simulation ticks, received properties, and prediction corrections. Those records answer different questions. A rendered location describes a view; a server result describes an accepted simulation step; a package entry locates stored content.

For your own mod, keep module versions explicit and record which side owns each value. Start work after DLL loading has finished, stop workers before unloading, and release their handles when stopping tools. For defenders, validate player requests against server-owned state and keep work per client bounded. Interpolation, quantization, and correction explain some ordinary discrepancies, so one mismatch needs context. Chapter 15 builds on this separation between requests, observations, and decisions.
